title: Reading a failure
objectives: Find the failing test in pytest's short and long reports
Read both values and the call from a failure report
Decide whether the code, the test or neither is at fault

screens.title: Which test caught it
screens.prose: Someone edited `returns.py` this morning. You run `pytest -v`, which prints one line per test with its result.
screens.question: Tap the test that caught the change.

hints.text: Look down the Result column.
One line does not say PASSED.

feedback.correct: `test_down_day` failed, so the change broke falls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line marked FAILED, then tap its test name.

byKey.r1c1: That is the right row. Tap the test's name, on the left, to name it.
byKey.r0c0: `test_up_day` passed. The edit did not change what it checks.
byKey.r2c0: `test_flat_day` passed. The edit did not change what it checks.
byKey.r3c0: `test_one_price` passed. The edit did not change what it checks.

explain.text: FAILED means an assert in `test_down_day` did not hold. The other three ran to the end, so whatever the edit broke, it is something only a fall exposes. Each name tells you which behaviour to look at.

screens.prose: `pytest -q` is shorter. It prints one character per test, in file order: `.` for a pass and `F` for a failure. This run printed `..F.F`.
screens.question: Tap the tests that failed.

hints.text: Write the five characters under the five tests, in order.
The third character is `F`.

feedback.correct: The third and fifth characters are `F`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each character of `..F.F` to the test in the same place.

byKey.count-dots: You picked the dots. A dot is a pass, `F` is a failure.
byKey.shifted: You are one place out. The first character is the first test, `test_up_day`.

explain.text: Lined up, `..F.F` puts `F` under `test_flat_day` and `test_two_days`. The short report says how many failed and where. The details come next, in the failure report.

screens.prose: Under the dots, pytest prints a **failure report** for each failed test. The `>` line is the assert that failed. The `E` lines show the values on both sides of `==`.
screens.question: What did `simple_return(100.00, 90.00)` actually return?

options.why: That is the hand answer written in the test. The `where` line names the value the call produced.
That is the line of the file where the assert sits: `test_returns.py:9`.
That is an argument passed in. The value before `=` on the `where` line is what came back.

hints.text: Find the line that starts `E        +  where`.
It reads: value `=` the call that produced it.

feedback.correct: The code gave −0.1111111111111111, the test expected −0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the `where` line: the value comes before `=`.

explain.text: pytest rewrites a failed `assert a == b` to show both sides: here −0.1111 against −0.1. The `where` line says the left side came from `simple_return(100.0, 90.0)`. Now you know the input, the output and the expected value.

screens.prose: The report gives you a clue: −0.1111 is what the code made of a fall from £100.00 to £90.00. Work out what each formula gives.
screens.question: Which formula is the edited code using?

options.text: (p1 − p0) / p1: it divides by the later price
(p1 − p0) / p0, the right formula
options.why: That gives −10 / 100 = −0.1, the test's hand answer. The code gave something else.

options.text: (p0 − p1) / p0: it subtracts the wrong way round
options.why: That gives +0.1: the right size with the wrong sign. The code's value was −0.1111.

options.text: None of them: it is a floating-point slip
options.why: Float slips are near 1e-17. This value is wrong in the second decimal place.

hints.text: −0.1111 is −10 divided by what?
Compute each formula for p0 = 100, p1 = 90.
−10 / 90 = −0.1111. Only the second formula divides by 90.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each formula for £100.00 to £90.00.

explain.text: −10 / 100 = −0.1, −10 / 90 = −0.1111 and 10 / 100 = 0.1. Only dividing by the later price matches the report. The failure gave you the numbers to work backwards from.

screens.prose: Another run, another report. This time look hard at both numbers before you touch the code.
screens.question: What needs fixing?

options.text: The test: £5.00 on £250.00 is 0.02, so the hand answer is wrong
The code: it should give 0.2
options.why: You trusted the test. Work it out: 5 / 250 is 0.02, which is what the code gave.

options.text: Both the code and the test
options.why: The code's 0.02 is right. Only the hand answer, 0.2, is off by a factor of ten.

options.text: Neither: run it again
options.why: The same inputs give the same output every run. It would fail the same way.

hints.text: Work out the return from £250.00 to £255.00 yourself.
Compare your answer with each side of `==`.
£5.00 / £250.00 = 0.02. The code agrees with you. The test does not.

feedback.correct: The code is right. The test's 0.2 was a slip by a factor of ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the true return, then see which side matches it.

byKey.code: You trusted the test. A failure says the two sides disagree, not which one is wrong. Here the code's 0.02 is right.

explain.text: £5.00 / £250.00 = 0.02, so the code is right and the test's hand answer is wrong. A failure means the code and the test disagree. Check your own working before you change the code.

screens.prose: One more failed test, `test_flat_day`. Its report looks different.

rows: E       NameError: name 'simple_retrun' is not defined

screens.question: What does this tell you about `simple_return` on a flat day?

options.text: Nothing: the call never happened, because of a typo in the test
It returns the wrong value for a flat day
options.why: You read every failure as a wrong answer. A `NameError` means Python could not find the function, so nothing was returned.

options.text: It is missing from `returns.py`
options.why: Look at the spelling in the error: `simple_retrun`. The typo is in the test, not the code.

options.text: It divides by zero on a flat day
options.why: A flat day has a zero change, not a zero price. That would also read `ZeroDivisionError`, not `NameError`.

hints.text: Read the last word of the report. Is it `AssertionError`?
The `E` line names the error and the name Python could not find.
`simple_retrun` swaps two letters. Python never reached `simple_return`.

feedback.correct: The test crashed before it asked the code anything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the error type on the `E` line.

byKey.wrong: You read every failure as a wrong answer. Here the `E` line is a `NameError`: the function was never called.

explain.text: A failed assert ends in `AssertionError` and shows two values. This report ends in `NameError`, with no values at all. The test is broken, so it tells you nothing about the code until you fix the typo.

screens.prose: You rename `test_returns.py` to `returns_tests.py` and run `pytest -q`. It prints a single line: `no tests ran in 0.01s`.
screens.question: What does this tell you about the code in `returns.py`?

options.text: Nothing: pytest found no tests to run
It is fine: nothing failed
options.why: No failures because nothing ran. Zero tests check zero behaviours.

options.text: It is broken: no tests passed
options.why: Nothing passed and nothing failed. The run never reached the code.

options.text: The file is empty
options.why: The file still holds every test. Its new name matches neither `test_*.py` nor `*_test.py`.

hints.text: Does `returns_tests.py` match `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`?
It ends in `_tests.py`, with an extra s, so pytest skips the file and runs nothing.

feedback.correct: No tests ran, so there is no verdict on the code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many tests pytest ran.

explain.text: `returns_tests.py` ends in `_tests`, so it matches neither pattern and nothing is collected. This edge case reads like silence, but it is not a pass. When the count is zero, check your names first.

screens.prose:
You read every report from the top down. The FAILED line names the test, `>` marks the assert, and the `E` lines give both values and the call.

```text
FAILED test_returns.py::test_down_day
>  assert simple_return(100.00, 90.00) == -0.1
E  assert -0.1111111111111111 == -0.1
E   +  where -0.1111111111111111 = ...
```

Then you work out the true answer yourself and decide which side is wrong.
screens.question: A test fails with `AssertionError`. What does that prove?

options.text: The code and the test disagree on one input
The code is wrong
options.why: Sometimes the hand answer is the slip, as with 0.2 for 0.02.

options.text: The code crashed
options.why: A crash shows a different error, such as `NameError`. `AssertionError` means the code ran and the values differed.

options.text: The code is wrong on every input
options.why: A test checks one input. Other inputs may be fine, as the passing tests showed.

hints.text: Think of the £250.00 report, where the code was right.
An `AssertionError` says the two sides of `==` differ. Your own working decides which side is wrong.

feedback.correct: A failure is a disagreement. Your working settles it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remember the report where the code was right and the test was not.

explain.text: An `AssertionError` says only that the two sides of `==` differed. You settle who is wrong by working the answer out yourself. Any other error type means the test never got that far.

screens.prose: A backtest reports **maximum drawdown**: the largest fall from a peak to a later low. It is a fraction of the peak, and prices are in pounds. Its tests:
screens.question: What is going on?

options.text: The code measures the whole range, ignoring that the low came before the high
The test is wrong: a steady rise has a drawdown
options.why: A drawdown needs a fall after a peak. A steady rise never falls, so 0.0 is the right answer.

options.text: A floating-point slip
options.why: 0.1736 is far too big for a slip, which would be near 1e-17.

options.text: The code cannot handle three prices
options.why: `test_flat` also uses three prices, and it passed.

hints.text: Does a steady rise ever fall from a peak?
21 / 121 = 0.1736. That is the gap between the lowest and highest price, though the low came first.

feedback.correct: (121 − 100) / 121 = 0.1736: the code treats the early low as a fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what (highest − lowest) / highest gives for 100, 110, 121.

byKey.test: A drawdown needs a fall after a peak. A steady rise never falls, so the test's 0.0 is right.

explain.text: (121 − 100) / 121 = 0.1736, so the code is measuring the whole range. In the dip test the high came before the low, so the bug hid. The steady-rise edge case exposed it, and the passing tests narrowed the search.

canvas.caption: 21 / 121 = 0.1736: the low came before the high

ideas: `pytest -q` prints `.` for each pass and `F` for each failure, in file order. `pytest -v` names each test with PASSED or FAILED.
A failure report shows the failing assert, both values, and the call that produced the left one.
`AssertionError` means the code and test disagree, so work out the answer to see who is wrong. Any other error means the test crashed first.

formula.name: Reading order
formula.note: Which test, which assert, both values, then who is right.

summary.trap: Not every failure is a wrong answer. A `NameError` in the test means the code was never asked.

quiz.prose: `pytest -q` prints `.F..F.F` and then the failure reports.
quiz.question: How many tests passed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the dots.

byKey.failed: That is the number of `F`s, the failures.
byKey.all: That is every test. Only the dots are passes.

explain.text: Each character is one test: `.` passed and `F` failed. Four dots and three `F`s make seven tests, and the summary line would read `3 failed, 4 passed`.

options.why: That is the hand answer in the test. The code's value is the left side of the `E` line.
Those are the prices passed in, on the `>` line.

options.text: Nothing: it crashed
options.why: A crash would end in an error such as `NameError`. Here the code returned a list.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the left side of `==` on the `E` line.

explain.text: The `E` line shows the returned list on the left of `==`. For lists, pytest adds the first index where they differ. 0.0909 is 10 / 110, so the code divides by the later price.

quiz.prose:
```text
>       assert simple_return(80.00, 60.00) == -0.20
E       assert -0.25 == -0.2
E        +  where -0.25 = simple_return(80.0, 60.0)
```
quiz.question: Which side is wrong?

options.text: The test: the return is −0.25
The code: the return is −0.20
options.why: You trusted the hand answer. The £20.00 fall divided by the starting £80.00 is −0.25, which is what the code gave.

options.text: Neither: they are close enough
options.why: −0.25 and −0.20 differ by five percentage points. That is a real disagreement.

feedback.correct: £20.00 down on £80.00 is −0.25, so the code is right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the return from £80.00 to £60.00 yourself.

explain.text: (60 − 80) / 80 = −20 / 80 = −0.25, which is what the code gave. The hand answer −0.20 is the slip, so fix the test.

quiz.prose: A failure report ends with `test_vol.py:7: TypeError`.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: Something raised `TypeError` before the assert could compare values
The vol function returned the wrong number
options.why: A wrong number ends in `AssertionError`, with both values shown. `TypeError` means an operation failed.

options.text: The test checked the type of the result and it was wrong
options.why: The report names the error that was raised. No assert about types failed here.

options.text: The test passed with a warning
options.why: A line in the failure report means the test failed.

feedback.correct: An error stopped the test before any comparison.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare this error type with `AssertionError`.

explain.text: `AssertionError` means the values differed. Any other error type, such as `TypeError` or `NameError`, means the test crashed on line 7 before it could compare.
